explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ishmael and his ten men come to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and they eat a meal together there (Jeremiah 41:1). Gedaliah had called the warning a lie, so he sat right down at the table with the man he was warned about. I think that meal had to be the quietest one ever served.

The text says the opposite, friend. Ishmael came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "and they ate a meal together there." (Jeremiah 41:1) Nobody stormed in swinging. They sat down and ate first, and that's what makes the next verse land so hard.

That's the one, baker. Ishmael killed "the Chaldean soldiers who were there" along with the Jews who were with Gedaliah (Jeremiah 41:3). Chaldeans is the name used here for the Babylonians, and Babylon's king was the one who had appointed Gedaliah. That detail matters later in this story.

Close on the map, but not the ones at Mizpah. The text says Ishmael killed the Chaldean soldiers who were there (Jeremiah 41:3). Egypt does come up later, but it's not the soldiers' home team here. Hang onto that word, friend, because it comes back.

The Philistines are a good guess for a soldier question, baker. But the text names the Chaldean soldiers at Mizpah as the ones Ishmael killed (Jeremiah 41:3). Chaldeans were the Babylonians, the same people whose king had appointed Gedaliah. No Philistines anywhere in this scene.

Right, baker. The eighty men were carrying grain offerings and frankincense "for the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 41:5) They had shaved their beards, torn their clothes and cut themselves, and they still made the trip with offerings in their hands. I think that tells you how much it mattered to them.

Babylon's palace is a long walk from Shechem, friend. The offerings were "for the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 41:5) These men came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, carrying grain offerings and frankincense toward the LORD's house.

Not Baal, baker. The text says the grain offerings and frankincense were for "the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 41:5) Baal was a false god, and these men weren't headed his way. They were bringing their offerings to the LORD's house.

That's it, baker. Ishmael "went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he went." (Jeremiah 41:6) The text tells us what he did, and it doesn't say why he did it. I think the tears were part of how he got those men to follow him, but that's my guess. And what he did to them next is heavy.

No laughing here, friend. The text says Ishmael went out "weeping as he went." (Jeremiah 41:6) And this is a heavy part of the story, so I'm keeping my jokes in the oven. Ishmael is crying on the road while Gedaliah already lies dead.

No songs on this road, baker. Ishmael went out to meet the eighty men "weeping as he went." (Jeremiah 41:6) That's a sad scene even before the next verse. Nobody there knew what was waiting at Mizpah.

explanations.answer: Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Ishmael said, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam." (Jeremiah 41:6) Gedaliah was already dead, and the eighty men didn't know it, since the text says no one yet knew (Jeremiah 41:4). The invitation sounded friendly, and that's what makes it so chilling.

explanations.answer: Turn back to your homes now
explanations.explanation: If only, friend. That would have saved those men. But what Ishmael actually said was, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam." (Jeremiah 41:6) He called them toward Gedaliah, who was already dead, and the text says they went into the city (Jeremiah 41:7).

Not quite, baker. The eighty men were already headed toward the house of the LORD (Jeremiah 41:5), so Ishmael didn't point them anywhere else. He said, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam." (Jeremiah 41:6) He pulled them toward Mizpah, and they didn't make it out.

Not this time, friend. Ten of the men told Ishmael, "Do not kill us, for we have hidden treasure in the field." The text says "So he refrained from killing them with the others." (Jeremiah 41:8) They spoke up and were spared. The other men weren't so fortunate.

Right, baker. The ten men said they had hidden treasure in the field, and the text says "So he refrained from killing them with the others." (Jeremiah 41:8) The ten were spared while the rest were killed. I think those ten had never talked so fast in their lives.

That's right, baker. Ishmael "set off to cross over to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:10) He took all the people left in Mizpah with him. The Ammonites were a nation east of the Jordan, so he was hauling his captives out of Judah.

Good guess on a long trip, friend, but no. The text says Ishmael "set off to cross over to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:10) He wasn't headed to Damascus. He was taking his captives out of Mizpah toward the Ammonites.

Moab is a neighbor, baker, but it's not the one here. The text says Ishmael "set off to cross over to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:10) The Ammonites were another nation across the river. Moab doesn't come up in this passage.

explanations.answer: Near the great pool in Gibeon
explanations.explanation: That's the spot, baker. Johanan and his men "found him near the great pool in Gibeon." (Jeremiah 41:12) Johanan, the army commander who had warned Gedaliah, caught up with Ishmael before he made it out of the land. Gibeon is where the chase ended.

Ishmael was headed for the Ammonites, so the river makes sense, friend. But he never got that far. The text says Johanan's men found him "near the great pool in Gibeon." (Jeremiah 41:12) Johanan caught him before he got away.

Not Jerusalem, baker. The text says they found Ishmael "near the great pool in Gibeon." (Jeremiah 41:12) He was still on his way to the Ammonites with his captives when Johanan caught up. Gibeon is where they finally met.

Yes, baker. "When all the people with Ishmael saw Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the army with him, they rejoiced." (Jeremiah 41:13) I bet that was the best sight those captives had seen in days. Help had finally come over the hill.

I'd have trembled too, friend, but that's not what the text says. The people with Ishmael "rejoiced" when they saw Johanan and the commanders (Jeremiah 41:13). I think they'd been waiting for someone, anyone, to show up. They got Johanan.

They did move, baker, but they didn't scatter. The text says they "rejoiced," and then they turned and went over to Johanan (Jeremiah 41:13-14). They all headed the same direction, straight toward their rescuers.

Not quite, friend. The text says "Ishmael son of Nethaniah and eight of his men escaped from Johanan." (Jeremiah 41:15) He came with ten men, and now he has eight. Ishmael got away, but he lost two on the way.

Right, baker. "Ishmael son of Nethaniah and eight of his men escaped from Johanan and went to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:15) He started with ten men, so two didn't make it out. Ishmael himself got away, and the captives didn't go with him.

That's the one, baker. They stayed at Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem, "in order to proceed into Egypt." (Jeremiah 41:17) The text says they planned to go, and the next verse tells us why they wanted out. Remember this word, because it matters for what comes next.

Edom is a neighbor, friend, but it's not their plan. The text says they stayed at Geruth Chimham "in order to proceed into Egypt." (Jeremiah 41:17) Egypt was the destination in their minds. They just hadn't left yet.
Wrong direction, baker. Johanan and the people stopped at Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem, "in order to proceed into Egypt." (Jeremiah 41:17) Assyria isn't in this passage at all. Egypt was the plan.

explanations.answer: Ishmael killed the governor Babylon appointed
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "They were afraid of the Chaldeans because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land." (Jeremiah 41:18) Ishmael did the killing, and the people were the ones who felt the fear. They wanted to get out of the way before Babylon came looking.

Johanan did fight, friend, but not against Babylon. He went to fight Ishmael (Jeremiah 41:12). The people feared the Chaldeans "because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land." (Jeremiah 41:18)

explanations.answer: The people stopped serving Babylon's king
explanations.explanation: Not in this passage, baker. The text gives one reason: "Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land." (Jeremiah 41:18) The people didn't rebel. They got scared because of what Ishmael did.
